directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Published work already shows that a model one tier down from the top forecasts research results about as well as the top one, and that much smaller models do worse. BrainBench (Luo et al., 2024, arXiv 2403.03230; Nature Human Behaviour) found that 7B models "performed comparably to larger models", while TinyLlama (1.1B) was "falling much behind the 7B models". SciPredict (arXiv 2604.10718, 2026) has Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 22.55% against Opus 4.5 at 23.05% and Llama 3.1 8B at 14.65%. Hewitt et al. (2024, working paper) found that accuracy "improved steadily and markedly across generations of LLMs". Ours agrees on the size pattern: Sonnet is not shown different from Opus (Brier 0.168 against 0.163; paired difference +0.004, interval −0.018 to +0.027) and Haiku is weaker (0.208; paired difference from Opus +0.044, interval +0.012 to +0.076). (2024, arXiv 2411.17595) found GPT-4o-mini predicting every clinical trial a success, a smaller same-family model collapsing onto a positive-outcome rule, but report no such rule as a baseline. So the result that Haiku beats a coin but is not shown to beat the good-news rule by the 0.01 margin, and that neither smaller model beats the flattery rater on round 2's items (a reported row), is new. directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** new. No published work I found reports that a valence question ("which version is better news for the paper's own idea?") solves BrainBench or any real-versus-altered results task. BrainBench (Luo et al., 2024, arXiv 2403.03230, *Nature Human Behaviour*) ran local-context, swapped-sentence, zlib-perplexity memorisation, publication-date, calibration and GPT-4-item controls, and found "no indication that BrainBench was memorized". It tests no valence, positive-result or publication-bias shortcut, and neither do its follow-ups (Luo, Sun and Love, 2024, arXiv 2405.09395; Luo, Ramscar and Love, 2024, arXiv 2411.11061) or Wen et al. (2025, arXiv 2506.00794, which checks "superficial features like idea complexity"). Lee (2026, arXiv 2604.06236) is not this test, and it does not mention BrainBench, valence or shortcuts. It proposes, without running anything (§5.5: "does not include empirical validation"), three things. §4.1: give LLMs only the starting information of 200–500 completed ClinicalTrials.gov trials, ask for a probability of success, and score with AUC-ROC and with the probabilities given to failed trials, hypothesising that "LLMs systematically overestimate the probability of experimental success". §4.2: compare five context conditions (none, successes only, failures only, both, failures classified by cause), with a dose-response at 10, 50, 100 and 200 failure records. §5.3: correlate "the published positive-result ratio and the actual success ratio (obtainable from trial registries)" across medical subfields, plus a peer-review test on OpenReview. So this project's earlier statement that ours is "the test an April 2026 paper asked for" (paper/novelty.md finding 8, ranked replication 1) overstates the link. The swap-both-orders-and-average fix and the first-position pull are known: Zheng et al. (2023, arXiv 2306.05685) found Claude-v1 consistent on swapped order 23.8% of the time and favouring the first answer 75.0%; Wang et al. (2023, arXiv 2305.17926, Balanced Position Calibration) average the scores over both orders. LLMs swayed by favourable framing is in print in another form (Yun et al., CHIL 2025, arXiv 2502.07963, spin in medical abstracts), but not as a rule for picking real results. What is new is only the headline, a one-line valence question beating the 63.4% for experts on BrainBench, and it cannot be told apart from memory or plausibility. directions.novelty_line: **Novelty:** partly new. Luo et al. (2024, arXiv 2403.03230 v4, *Nature Human Behaviour*) prompted no model for an answer: "A correct response was when the model produces a lower perplexity for the original abstract than the altered abstract", each abstract prefixed only with "You are a neuroscientist with deep knowledge in neuroscience", on open models only (Llama-2 7B to 70B and chat, Mistral-7B and instruct, Falcon-40B and 180B and their instruct/chat versions, Galactica 6.7B to 120B, TinyLlama 1.1B, Phi-3 3.8B, GPT-2 trained from scratch, BrainGPT; GPT-4 only wrote the 100 extra items, and Claude is not mentioned); it reports "LLMs averaging 81.4% accuracy and human experts averaging 63.4%", Phi-3 the best named model at 82.5%, and BrainGPT 3% above its base model. Its controls were local context only, swapped sentences, zlib-perplexity memorisation ("no indication that BrainBench was memorized"), publication date, calibration and the GPT-4-written items; it ran none for valence, flattery, positive results or option order (perplexity scores each version on its own), and it avoided prompting because "Prompting in natural language may yield less reliable judgments and degrade model competency", having found that "Chat or instruction-optimized models performed worse than their base model counterparts". The kind of result is in print elsewhere: Chen, Hu and Lu (2025, arXiv 2504.01167) prompted GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o to pick a real field-experiment conclusion from among itself, a reversed variant and an unrelated variant (best 78%, GPT-4o with chain of thought), and found that the conclusion's sentiment label predicted accuracy only in interaction with some topics (for example ethnicity); Liu and Shah (2023, arXiv 2306.00622) found GPT-4 "biased towards the abstract that has a positive (p<0.05) result" in one constructed pair; and in metascience terms, Fanelli (2012, *Scientometrics* 90:891–904) found that 85.9% of 2007 papers that tested a hypothesis reported support for it, a base rate a "better news" rule could exploit. No paper found reports a prompted Claude or GPT-4-class model on BrainBench, a valence-only question solving a real-versus-altered results task, or that question's gap to a direct forecasting prompt; so what is new here is only that comparison: Opus 89.4% with the valence question and 95.2% asked directly, with a similar gap on Sonnet (+6.3 points) and one not shown on Haiku (+5.3, interval including zero). This disagrees with ss-b10c's "new", whose search missed Chen et al., and it cannot separate valence from memory or plausibility.
